countries.text: Palladius (431) and Patrick (5th century) established bishops; by the sixth century a dense network of monasteries made Ireland a Christian society and a sending base.
Sub-Roman British Christianity produced monastic leaders such as David (d. c. 589), Illtud and Samson, who exchanged monks with Ireland and Brittany.
British monks and emigrants (Samson of Dol, Paul Aurelian) Christianised Armorica; Columbanus landed here c. 590.
Columba founded Iona in 563 and visited the Pictish king Bridei; Iona's monasteries gradually Christianised the Picts.
Columbanus founded Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine; Luxeuil's rule and alumni spread to some fifty monasteries across Gaul.
Columbanus preached at Tuggen and Bregenz; Gall's hermitage became St Gallen. Fridolin is associated with Säckingen.
Columbanus founded Bobbio with the Lombard king Agilulf's grant; it became a major library and opposed Lombard Arianism.
Aidan and the Iona monks re-evangelised Northumbria after Paulinus's mission collapsed; Cedd and Chad took the faith to Essex and Mercia.
The Irish bishop Kilian and companions preached in Thuringian-ruled Würzburg and were killed c. 689.
Irish hermits (papar) reached the Faroes and Iceland before the Norse; the geographer Dicuil (825) describes them.

journeys.title: Patrick: captivity, escape and return (traditional sites)

stops.name: Western Britain (home; site of Bannavem Taburniae unknown)

journeys.text: Patrick's own Confessio gives the outline — capture at about sixteen, six years of slavery, escape by ship, return as bishop — but no place-names in Ireland. The sites shown (Slemish, Saul, Armagh, Croagh Patrick, Downpatrick) and the dates 432–461 come from later tradition and annals.

journeys.title: Columba: Derry to Iona and the Picts
journeys.text: In 563 Columba settled on Iona in Dál Riata. Adomnán's Life describes his journey up the Great Glen to the Pictish king Bridei son of Maelchon, the famous encounter with a beast in the River Ness, and his death on Iona in 597.

journeys.title: Columbanus: Bangor to Bobbio
journeys.people: Columbanus with twelve companions, including Gall
journeys.text: Jonas of Bobbio's Life (c. 640) records Columbanus's founding of monasteries in the Vosges, his expulsion by Theuderic II and Brunhild, the storm that drove the deportation ship back at Nantes, his mission among the Alemanni at Bregenz, and his final foundation at Bobbio, where he died in 615.

journeys.title: Aidan: Iona to Lindisfarne
journeys.text: At King Oswald's request Iona sent Aidan, who established his see on the tidal island of Lindisfarne beside Bamburgh and toured Northumbria on foot; he died at Bamburgh in 651.

relations.text: Irish and Roman missions together converted the English; Irish-trained Englishmen such as Egbert (at Rath Melsigi) sent Willibrord to Frisia, and Iona and Canterbury traditions fused after Whitby (664). After Whitby the Northumbrian church adopted Roman Easter and organisation, and Irish monastic ideals were absorbed into the Anglo-Saxon continental mission.

agreements.text: Shared Latin creed, Scriptures, monastic ideals and loyalty to the papacy; Bede admired Aidan's holiness, and Anglo-Saxon missionaries adopted the Irish ideal of peregrinatio.

disagreements.text: Clashed over the date of Easter, the form of tonsure and episcopal authority: Augustine failed to win the British bishops c. 603, and at Whitby (664) Wilfrid's Roman party defeated Colman's Ionan party.
Columbanus at Bobbio opposed the Arianism still held by part of the Lombard nobility.

deviations: The ascetic ideal of poverty and exile coexisted with monasteries that grew rich, held slaves and became instruments of dynastic power, with abbacies passing within ruling families.
Columbanus's refusal to submit to local bishops and his insistence on Irish Easter put him at odds with church order as generally understood.
Modern ‘Celtic Christianity’ movements have projected later romantic, environmental or anti-Roman ideals onto these missions that the sources do not support.

missions.name: Gregory's mission to the English and the Anglo-Saxon mission to Germany (Augustine, Willibrord, Boniface)
missions.statusNote: The English church founded by Gregory's mission became, within a century, a missionary church in its own right. Its continental missions merged into the Carolingian church of the Franks; the evangelisation of Saxony was completed by Charlemagne's conquest, and the model passed to the ninth-century missions to Scandinavia.
missions.summary: In 596 Pope Gregory the Great sent the monk Augustine with about forty companions to the pagan English; landing in Kent in 597, they baptised King Æthelberht and founded the see of Canterbury. A century later English monks, inspired by Irish peregrinatio and loyal to Rome, carried the faith to their continental ‘kinsmen’: Willibrord to Frisia (690) and Boniface to Hesse, Thuringia and Bavaria (719–754). Their work, intertwined with Frankish power, shaped the medieval German church — and stands in contrast to the forced conversion of Saxony under Charlemagne.
missions.story:
According to a story Bede already reports as tradition, Gregory saw fair-haired English slave boys in the Roman market and resolved to evangelise their people (‘not Angles but angels’). Whatever its truth, in 596 Gregory, now pope, dispatched Augustine, prior of his own monastery of St Andrew, with about forty monks. Frightened by tales of English savagery, they halted in Provence and Augustine returned to Rome to ask to be released; Gregory sent them on with letters to Frankish bishops and rulers. They landed on the Isle of Thanet in 597 and were received by Æthelberht of Kent, whose Frankish Christian queen Bertha already worshipped with her chaplain Liudhard at St Martin's church in Canterbury. Æthelberht was baptised, probably in 597, and Gregory reported to Alexandria that more than 10,000 English had been baptised at Christmas 597.

Gregory's letters show a carefully thought-out strategy. A plan for two metropolitan sees (London and York) with twelve bishops each envisaged a complete church structure. In his famous letter to Abbot Mellitus (601), Gregory reversed earlier advice to destroy temples and instead directed that they be purified and turned into churches and that pagan feasts be replaced by Christian festivals — ‘for he who would climb to a lofty height must go up by steps, not leaps’. Augustine's attempt to bring the British (Welsh) bishops under his authority failed at ‘Augustine's Oak’ c. 603, and Bede later presented the slaughter of the monks of Bangor-is-y-Coed by the pagan Æthelfrith at Chester (c. 615) as divine judgement on the British refusal.

The conversion of the English kingdoms took nearly a century and suffered reverses. After Æthelberht's death (616) Kent and Essex relapsed for a time. Paulinus baptised King Edwin of Northumbria at York at Easter 627 and conducted mass baptisms in the rivers Glen and Swale, but fled south after Edwin's death in battle (633). Northumbria was re-evangelised from Iona under Aidan (635); Birinus, sent by Pope Honorius, converted Wessex (635); Felix, a Burgundian, worked in East Anglia. Mercia's pagan king Penda allowed preaching but remained pagan until his death (655). The Synod of Whitby (664) aligned Northumbria with Roman customs, and Archbishop Theodore of Tarsus (669–690) organised the dioceses and founded a school at Canterbury. Sussex was the last kingdom to be converted, by the exiled Wilfrid c. 681–686; when the West Saxon king Cædwalla conquered the Isle of Wight (686) he tried, in Bede's words, to wipe out its native inhabitants and replace them with his own people, giving a quarter of the island to Wilfrid.

By 700 the English church, with scholars such as Aldhelm and Bede and monasteries such as Wearmouth-Jarrow, began to send missionaries to the continental Saxons and Frisians, whom it regarded as kin. Wilfrid preached in Frisia in 678–679; the Northumbrian Egbert, living in exile in Ireland, organised a mission and in 690 sent Willibrord with eleven companions from Rath Melsigi. Willibrord worked in the zone conquered by the Frankish mayor Pippin II, was consecrated archbishop of the Frisians in Rome in 695 with the name Clement, set his see at Utrecht and founded Echternach (698). The pagan Frisian king Radbod's resistance and Willibrord's dependence on Frankish arms limited his success; an attempt to reach Denmark achieved little.

Wynfreth of Wessex, renamed Boniface by Pope Gregory II in 719, became the greatest of the Anglo-Saxon missionaries. After failing in Frisia (716), he received a papal commission (719), worked with Willibrord, and then evangelised Hesse and Thuringia, where many already had a syncretistic, half-Christian practice. At Geismar (723), under the protection of Charles Martel, he felled the sacred oak of Donar and used its timber for a chapel — a demonstration of the powerlessness of the old gods recorded by his biographer Willibald. He founded monasteries (Fritzlar, Ohrdruf, Fulda in 744 with Sturm), invited English women such as Leoba, Thecla and Walburga to lead convents, organised the Bavarian dioceses (739) and new sees at Würzburg, Büraburg and Erfurt (741–742), and presided with Carloman over the reforming Concilium Germanicum (742/743). His letters show deep reliance on Frankish power — he admitted that without the prince's protection he could neither govern his people nor prevent pagan rites — and also on English friends, who sent books and advice. In old age he returned to Frisia and was killed with some fifty companions by robbers or pagans at Dokkum on 5 June 754.

Boniface's persuasion-under-protection contrasts sharply with what followed. Charlemagne's Saxon Wars (772–804) began with the destruction of the Irminsul shrine and were fought as both conquest and conversion. The Royal Frankish Annals record the beheading of 4,500 Saxons at Verden in 782 (a figure some historians doubt), and the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae (c. 782–785) prescribed death for refusing baptism, cremating the dead or eating meat in Lent. The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin, Charlemagne's adviser, protested in 796 that ‘faith arises from the will, not from compulsion’ and that imposing tithes on new converts was wrecking the mission. Missionaries such as the Northumbrian Willehad (Bremen, 787) and the Frisian Liudger (Münster, d. 809), trained at York, worked within this coerced settlement and tried to make it real. Saxony became Christian, and a century later Saxon kings led the Christian empire — but the method left a long shadow over the history of mission.
beliefs: Latin Catholic orthodoxy under the authority of the bishop of Rome, to whom Boniface swore an oath of obedience in 722.
The necessity of baptism for salvation, and the duty of rulers to promote the true faith and suppress idolatry.
Canonical order: bishops in fixed sees, regular synods, clerical celibacy and correct liturgy according to Roman usage.
The Benedictine monastic life as the backbone of the church and of mission.
Gradual transformation of pagan custom where possible (Gregory to Mellitus) alongside firm rejection of sacrifice, divination and sacred groves and trees.
A sense of kinship obligation: the English owed the gospel to their continental Germanic relatives.
strategies: Conversion of kings first, using royal marriages (Bertha in Kent, Æthelburh in Northumbria) and Frankish diplomatic support.
Papal commissioning and close correspondence with Rome; the pallium and diocesan plans issued from Rome.
Adaptation of pagan temples and festivals (Gregory's letter of 601) while condemning sacrifice.
Dramatic demonstrations of the impotence of pagan gods, such as Boniface's felling of the oak at Geismar (723).
Founding monasteries and convents as schools, libraries and centres of agriculture (Wearmouth-Jarrow, Echternach, Fulda, Tauberbischofsheim).
Building episcopal structures and reforming synods to discipline clergy and suppress syncretism.
Networks of English supporters who supplied books, manpower and prayer, including women correspondents such as Eadburga and Bugga.
groupsReached: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms: Kent, Essex, Northumbria, East Anglia, Wessex, Mercia and Sussex.
Frisians in the coastal Low Countries.
Hessians and Thuringians in central Germany, many already partly Christian.
Bavarians and Alemanni, whose existing church Boniface reorganised.
Continental Saxons, forcibly Christianised under Charlemagne (772–804).
The Frankish clergy and nobility, targets of Boniface's reforms.
challenges: Pagan reactions after the deaths of Christian kings (Kent and Essex in 616, Northumbria in 633).
Resistance by the British church to Augustine's authority and later the Irish-Roman Easter dispute.
Frisian and Saxon resistance, tied to opposition to Frankish expansion (Radbod; Widukind).
Syncretism among nominal Christians and poorly trained or immoral Frankish clergy.
Dependence on the shifting politics of Frankish mayors and kings.
Violence: Boniface and his companions were killed at Dokkum (754); missionaries were killed in Saxon revolts.
harms: Charlemagne's conversion of the Saxons by conquest involved mass killings (Verden, 782), deportations and the Capitulatio's death penalty for refusing baptism or pagan practices — a model of coerced conversion that Alcuin himself criticised.
Even Boniface's mission relied on Frankish military protection; missionary success advanced alongside, and helped legitimise, Frankish conquest of Frisia, Hesse and Thuringia.
Bede's history presented the massacre of British monks at Chester (c. 615) as just punishment for refusing Augustine, illustrating hostility toward the native British church.
Cædwalla's conquest of the Isle of Wight (686) combined forced baptism with attempted extermination of its inhabitants, and the church accepted a quarter of the island as spoils.
Sacred sites and practices were destroyed (the Geismar oak, the Irminsul), and the heavy imposition of tithes on new converts provoked resentment and revolt.
Boniface denounced and helped condemn rival missionaries and clergy such as Aldebert and Clement as heretics, and his reforms were used to entrench clerical and papal control.
developments: The conversion of the English and the foundation of an organised English church centred on Canterbury and York.
Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731), Wearmouth-Jarrow learning and Theodore's school at Canterbury.
The first large-scale ‘second-generation’ mission: a newly converted people sending missionaries abroad.
The diocesan and monastic framework of the German church (Utrecht, Mainz, Würzburg, Fulda, Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg, Passau).
Reform of the Frankish church, preparing for the Carolingian renaissance in which Alcuin played a leading part.
A prominent role for women religious, such as Leoba, as leaders of mission convents.
missions.outcome: The Anglo-Saxon mission turned a recently pagan people into a missionary church within a century, laid the foundations of the German and Dutch churches, and bound them closely to Rome. Its last phase, the Christianisation of Saxony by the sword, raised an enduring question about the use of state force in mission.

countries.text: Augustine landed at Thanet, baptised Æthelberht and founded Canterbury; Rochester and London followed in 604.
Paulinus baptised King Edwin at York (627); after a pagan reaction, the Ionan mission and later Wilfrid and Theodore consolidated the church.
The British bishops refused Augustine's authority at ‘Augustine's Oak’ c. 603; Welsh churches accepted the Roman Easter only in 768.
Birinus converted Wessex (635); Mercia became Christian after Penda (655); Wilfrid converted Sussex (c. 681–686), the last pagan kingdom.
Willibrord's mission from 690 under Pippin II's protection; the see of Utrecht founded 695. Boniface was killed at Dokkum in 754.
Willibrord founded Echternach abbey (698), a base and scriptorium for the Frisian mission.
Willibrord's brief visit to the Danish king Ongendus (c. 710s) produced no lasting church; the Danish mission resumed with Anskar in 826.
Boniface's base: Amöneburg (721), Geismar oak (723), Fritzlar, Ohrdruf, the sees of Büraburg, Erfurt and Würzburg, and Fulda (744).
Boniface, as papal legate, reorganised the existing Bavarian church into the dioceses of Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg and Passau (739).
With Carloman and Pippin, Boniface held reform councils (742–747) and became archbishop of Mainz c. 746.
Conquered and forcibly Christianised in Charlemagne's Saxon Wars (772–804); Willehad (Bremen, 787) and Liudger (Münster) organised the new church.

journeys.title: Augustine's mission: Rome to Canterbury
journeys.text: Gregory's letters of commendation to the bishops and rulers of Gaul trace the route through Provence and up the Rhône and Loire. After Augustine's return to Rome to plead for release, the party continued, acquired Frankish interpreters, and landed on Thanet in 597 (Bede 1.23–25).

journeys.title: Paulinus to Northumbria
journeys.people: Paulinus with Queen Æthelburh of Kent
journeys.text: Paulinus accompanied the Christian princess Æthelburh to marry Edwin, baptised the king at York at Easter 627, baptised crowds for 36 days at the royal vill of Yeavering and preached in Lindsey, but fled back to Kent when Edwin fell at Hatfield Chase (633).

journeys.title: Willibrord: Ripon, Ireland, Frisia
journeys.text: Trained at Ripon under Wilfrid and for twelve years among the English exiles in Ireland, Willibrord was sent by Egbert to Frisia in 690. Consecrated archbishop in Rome in 695, he based his church at Utrecht and his monastery at Echternach, where he died in 739.

journeys.title: Boniface: Wessex to Dokkum
journeys.text: After a failed start in Frisia (716), Boniface went to Rome, was commissioned by Gregory II (719), assisted Willibrord, and then evangelised Hesse and Thuringia, felling the oak at Geismar in 723. As archbishop and legate he organised the Bavarian and central German dioceses, founded Fulda and took the see of Mainz. He returned to Frisia in old age and was killed at Dokkum on 5 June 754 (Willibald, Life of Boniface).

relations.text: Roman and Irish missions jointly converted the English; English missionaries to the continent were trained partly in Ireland and took up the Irish ideal of exile for Christ.

agreements.text: Shared monastic ideals and Latin learning; Bede praised Aidan, and Boniface valued Irish-trained colleagues while insisting on Roman canonical order.

disagreements.text: Augustine's demands that the British church adopt Roman Easter and baptismal practice failed (c. 603); the Roman party prevailed over the Ionan party at Whitby (664). Boniface also clashed with independent Irish-influenced clergy such as Clement and with Virgil of Salzburg.
Bavarian bishops of the sees Boniface had organised (Salzburg, Passau) opposed Methodius's Slavonic liturgy in Moravia and Pannonia and imprisoned him (870–873).

deviations: Gregory's patient, adaptive approach and Boniface's preaching under protection gave way under Charlemagne to conversion by conquest and capital punishment for paganism — opposed at the time by Alcuin.
A mission begun by monks vowed to poverty became closely tied to royal and aristocratic power, landholding and tithes.
The ideal of the church's independence was compromised by reliance on Frankish rulers, whom Boniface admitted he could not do without.
Insistence on uniform Roman practice led to the condemnation of fellow Christians — the British church and dissenting continental clergy — rather than cooperation.
